name: Postman
summary: Postman builds an API platform that developers use to design, test, document and monitor APIs, and it started in Bengaluru. Candidates commonly report a recruiter screen, a coding or practical exercise, and interviews on design and collaboration, with its five published values (Create with curiosity, Earn trust, Embrace constraints, Win together, Own & deliver) shaping the behavioral questions.
rounds: Coding round or a practical exercise, often close to real work
Technical deep dive on your past projects
System or API design round for experienced roles
looks_for: Good API design sense: clear contracts, versioning and error handling

questions.text: Tell me about a time you questioned an accepted best practice. What did you find?
covers: The practice and why you doubted it in your context
How you tested your doubt rather than just arguing
What you and the team changed, or why you kept it

questions.text: Describe a time you listened first and changed your plan because of what you heard.
covers: Your original plan and who you asked for input
What they told you that you hadn't considered
How the changed plan worked out, and what it did for trust

questions.text: Tell me about something good you shipped with less time, people or budget than you wanted.
covers: The constraint and the goal you still had to meet
What you cut, reused or simplified
The result and what the constraint taught you

questions.text: Tell me about a mistake you made at work and how you adapted afterwards.
covers: The mistake, owned clearly
How you fixed the immediate problem
What you now do differently, with an example

questions.text: Describe a time you helped a teammate succeed even though it slowed down your own task.
covers: What the teammate needed and why it mattered to the team
What you gave up and how you managed it
The outcome for the team

questions.text: What makes a REST API easy to use? Walk me through an API you'd consider well designed.
covers: Consistent resource names, HTTP methods and status codes
Helpful error messages, pagination and authentication that's easy to get right
Good docs and examples, with a real API you've used

questions.text: How would you design a feature that runs a collection of API tests on a schedule and alerts the team when they fail?
covers: A scheduler, workers that run tests in isolation, and stored results
Running from several regions, timeouts and retries for flaky endpoints
Alerting that's useful: grouping failures, avoiding noise, linking to the failed request

questions.text: How would you let two people edit the same API request at once without overwriting each other's changes?
covers: Options: locking, last-write-wins, operational transforms or CRDTs, and their trade-offs
Showing who else is editing, and handling offline edits
Keeping a history so changes can be reviewed or undone

questions.text: How would you version an API that many external clients depend on without breaking them?
covers: Additive changes first; what counts as a breaking change
A versioning scheme (path, header) and a deprecation timeline
Telling clients early, and measuring who still uses the old version

questions.text: Explain the difference between REST, GraphQL and gRPC, and when you'd pick each.
covers: REST: simple and cacheable, resources over HTTP
GraphQL: clients ask for exactly the fields they need
gRPC: fast, typed calls between services; a real case where you'd choose each

questions.text: A new desktop app release is crashing for some users. How would you find the cause and respond?
covers: Limiting the damage first: pause the rollout or roll back
Using crash reports to find what the affected users share: OS, version, settings
Fixing, testing on the affected setup, and telling users what happened

questions.text: How would you find out whether developers are getting value from a new feature in its first weeks?
covers: Usage that signals value, such as repeat use, not just first clicks
Talking to a few users and reading community feedback
A decision you'd make from the results: improve, promote or rethink

questions.text: Why Postman? How have you used it, or tools like it, in your own work?
covers: Specific use: testing, debugging, documenting or sharing APIs
What you like and one thing you'd improve
Why building for developers appeals to you

questions.text: Which of Postman's values do you relate to most, and when have you lived it?
covers: One value, named once
A short story that shows it in action
Why that way of working suits you

tips: Use Postman properly before the interview: build a collection, write a test script, and try a mock server or monitor.
Talk about developer experience: clear errors, good docs and sensible defaults matter as much as features.
Prepare a story for each of the five values; Embrace constraints suits a time-boxed or low-budget project.
In design rounds, think about teams: Postman is used for collaboration, so sync, sharing and permissions matter.
